corrections.label: Augmented sixth chord

before.card: An augmented sixth chord places two voices a semitone on either side of the dominant scale degree. The raised fourth moves upward while the lowered sixth moves downward toward that goal. This converging chromatic motion explains the chord family's predominant role in the cited tonal framework.
before.claim_review: Puget Sound 21.1 gives raised fourth, lowered sixth and simultaneous approach to five; the paragraph describes scale-degree tendencies, not an unrestricted claim about every voicing or historical style.
before.relation_note: Both are chromatic predominant devices, but their pitch construction differs: converging semitones versus a lowered-supertonic major triad.

after.card: An augmented sixth chord contains notes a semitone below and above the dominant scale degree. The raised fourth moves upward while the lowered sixth moves downward toward dominant pitches. This characteristic voice-leading explains the chord family's predominant role in the cited tonal framework.
after.claim_review: Puget Sound 21.1 states simultaneous semitone approaches to scale degree five and predominant function. Revised wording avoids describing the voices as converging in register; it only states the supported pitch-class movements.
after.relation_note: Both are chromatic predominant devices, but their construction differs: semitone approaches to dominant pitches versus a lowered-supertonic major triad.

corrections.reason: Remove potentially misleading convergence language, which could suggest that the augmented-sixth voices move toward the same register.

corrections.label: Eternalism

before.card: Eternalism holds that past and future objects exist as well as present ones. Existing need not mean being located at the present time, just as occupying another place need not mean being nowhere. The view separates an object's temporal location from whether it belongs to reality.
before.claim_review: SEP Time section 6 separates ontological existence from present temporal location and includes past/future objects; the spatial comparison restates the distinction, not a claim that all eternalists endorse one spacetime theory.

after.card: Eternalism holds that past and future objects exist as well as present ones. An object can belong to reality without occupying the present moment. The disagreement with presentism concerns what exists, rather than whether past events are now occurring or can presently be observed.
after.claim_review: SEP Time section 6 separates ontological existence from temporal location and includes past and future objects. The card avoids an extra spatial analogy and does not claim past events are happening at the present time.

corrections.reason: Keep the explanatory distinction directly within the source’s temporal-location discussion.

corrections.label: Rule of lenity

before.card: The rule of lenity favors the defendant when a criminal statute remains ambiguous. It concerns interpreting the reach of a penal law, rather than deciding whether evidence proves the alleged conduct. Its rationale includes reserving the definition of crimes and punishments to lawmakers instead of judicial expansion.

after.card: In US criminal law, lenity favors the defendant when a statute remains ambiguous. It concerns interpreting a penal law's reach, rather than deciding whether evidence proves the conduct. Its rationale includes reserving the definition of crimes and punishments to lawmakers instead of judicial expansion.

corrections.reason: Make the cited US legal setting explicit rather than imply every jurisdiction applies an identical doctrine.

corrections.label: Claim preclusion

before.card: Claim preclusion generally prevents a party from relitigating a cause of action after a final judgment on its merits. A losing plaintiff cannot simply sue the same defendant again on that claim; a winning plaintiff likewise cannot start another suit just to obtain additional recovery.

after.card: In US litigation, claim preclusion generally prevents repeating a cause of action after a final judgment on its merits. A losing plaintiff cannot simply sue the same defendant again on that claim; a winning plaintiff likewise cannot start another suit just to obtain additional recovery.

corrections.reason: Make jurisdiction explicit while retaining the general statement and both bar/merger examples.

corrections.label: Issue preclusion

before.card: Issue preclusion prevents relitigation of a factual or legal issue already validly, finally and necessarily decided in an earlier proceeding. It can matter even when the later lawsuit is a different claim. The focus is the resolved issue, rather than a wholesale repetition of the original action.

after.card: In US litigation, issue preclusion bars repeating a factual or legal issue already validly, finally and necessarily decided in an earlier proceeding. It can matter even when a later lawsuit is a different claim. The focus is the resolved issue, rather than repetition of the original action.

corrections.reason: Make the cited US litigation setting explicit without treating the concise definition as an exhaustive universal test.
